The adrenal glands #1

CT anatomy #2

  • Y-shaped

MRI #3

  • Hypointense relative to the liver

Pathology #4

  • Tumors
  • Primary
  •  benign:
  • - of cortical origin: cysts, adenomas
  • - of medullary orgin: pheochromocytoma
  • malignant – adenocarcinoma, malignant pheochromocytoma
  • Secondary : metastases (lung, kidney, lymphoma, breast)

Notes: Adrenal masses are seen in 1% of CT-examinations. Most of these masses are benign. Even in patients with a known malignancy these masses are usually non-functioning adenomas. The issue is how to differentiate these benign adenomas from malignant adrenal masses.

Adenomas #5

  • - 70% contain intracellular fat (low CT density)- Rapid contrast wash-out

Notes: Usually detected in post-menopausal women as an incidental finding. Most of them are non-functional and have an important fatty component which determines the hypodense, fatty appearance on CT ( ROI -100, -60, -16 HU). If it is under 20 HU, chance of malignancy is very low. If the lesion size is under 2cm, chance of malignancy is low. If post-contrast lesions enhance homogeneously and not too much, and important to remember, if the contrast washes-out rapidly than malignancy chance is very low.

Metastases #7

  • Lung!!!

Slide 9 #9

Notes: Adenoma on the right is homogeneously of low density. Metastasis on the left is inhomogeneous and centrally of low attenuation due to necrosis.

Myelolipoma #10

Notes: Contains hematopoietic cells and fat Right adrenal mass. Although it is inhomogeneous the fact that it has fatty inclusions (dark-hypodense-minus 100 HU-fat) is reassuring

Adrenal cyst #11

Notes: Large left adrenal mass, homogeneously hypodense with a density comparable with that of water, non-enhancing inner structure or rim Cysts may be of any size and in most instances are unilateral. Large cysts may be complicated by hemorrhage and consequent onset of acute symptoms. Pathological substrates include epithelial , endothelial, parasitic, and pseudocysts. Most importantly lesions show a thin wall and no enhancement after intravenous contast material.

Adrenal hemorrhage #12

Notes: Bilateral hyperdensities (80 HU)

Adrenal tuberculosis #13

Notes: Left adrenal mass with lots of suspicious, so called malignant features including size, inhomogeneity, calcifications, but is TB. That why is important to have patient history before imaging assessment.

Adenocarcinoma #14

Notes: Large mass, inhomogeneous. The big central hypodensity=necrosis

Adenocarcinoma #15

Notes: Left adrenal mass, more than 2cm in size, obviously inhomogeneous, with hypodense areas and calcification, with significant enhancement

Suspicious features #16

  • Other malignant tumors
  • Size > 2cm
  • Density > 20 HU
  • Heterogeneous structure
  • Significant enhancement with slow wash-out

Slide 17 #17

Notes: Left adrenal abnormality: ovoid mass, hypodense, homogeneous internal structure, less than 2cm in maximum diameter-most probably an adenoma. If the patient is known with a cancer, than it is mandatory at least a short term follow-up. Adrenals are not routinely biopsied due to increased risk of hemorrhage.

Normal bladder #33

Notes: Differential diagnosis for bladder wall thickening depends on whether the bladder is adequately distended. The bladder wall may be thickened if: >3 mm when distended >5 mm when nondistended If the bladder is not distended, then it is difficult to exclude artifactual thickening from a collapsed bladder If the bladder wall is adequately distended, then a differential may be developed based on whether the bladder is diffusely thickened or focally thickened

Thickening of the bladder wall #34

  • Diffuse bladder wall thickening
  • bladder outlet obstruction
  • neurogenic bladder
  • infectious cystitis
  • cystitis from radiation or chemotherapy
  • Focal bladder wall thickening
  • urothelial cell carcinoma of the bladder (transitional cell carcinoma)
  • artifact: blood products / clot will not enhance on postcontrast CT or MRI; no vascularity on colour Doppler. It may be adherent to the bladder wall, like tumour, but a clot is more likely to have a concave margin, unlike tumor
  • other bladder neoplasm
  • adjacent inflammatory process (e.g. diverticulitis)

Benign prostatic hyperplasia #46

Notes: BPH usually starts from the transitional zone Ultrasound has become the standard first line investigation after the urologist's finger. there is an increase in volume of the prostate with a calculated volume exceeding 30 mL (width x height x length x 0.52) the central gland is enlarged, and is hypoechoic or of mixed echogenicity calcification may be seen both within the enlarged gland as well as in the pseudocapsule (representing compressed peripheral zone) post-micturition residual volume is typically elevated 1: axial 2: sagital 3: transrectal

Slide 47 #47

US #48

Prostate cancer #49

  • Size measurement: transabdominal US
  • Superior resolution: endorectal US
  • A normal prostate US does not rule out cancer
  • Diagnosis = transrectal biopsy
  • Most sensitive detection and local staging technique= MRI
  • Metastases  CT

Prostate adenocarcinoma #50

Notes: Starts from the peripheral zone Ultrasound On ultrasound, prostate cancer is usually seen as a hypoechoic lesion (60-70%) in the peripheral zone of the gland, but can be hyperechoic or isoechoic (30-40% of lesions). Transrectal ultrasound is also the modality of choice for directing brachytherapy seeds into the prostate gland.

MRI: PI-RADS (prostate imaging reporting and data system) #51

Notes: Prostate cancer appears hypointense on T2 sequences The primary indication for MRI of the prostate is in the evaluation of prostate cancer after an ultrasound guided prostate biopsy has confirmed cancer in order to determine if there is extracapsular extension 1-2,4. Increasingly MRI is also being used to detect and localise cancer when the PSA is persistently elevated, but routine TRUS biopsy is negative. Both the American College of Radiology (ACR) and European Society of Uroradiology (ESUR) advocate the use of multiparametric-MRI in prostate imaging

Transrectal biopsy #52

Notes: Transrectal ultrasonography (TRUS) is often initially performed to detect abnormalities and to guide biopsy, usually following an abnormal PSA level or DRE. Ultrasound is used to direct biopsy of suspicious, hypoechoic regions, usually in the peripheral zone. Because of the high incidence of multifocality, systematic sextant biopsies are recommended.

Slide 62 #62

Notes: Stage IVA cervical carcinoma in a 60-year-old woman. (a) Sagittal and (b) coronal T2-weighted images show a large hyperintense mass that involves the entire circumference of the uterine cervix with involvement of the entire stromal thickness; parametrial infiltration is evidenced by irregular myometrial/ parametrial interface, and involvement of the vaginal fornices is present as evidenced by the loss of T2W signal intensity (short arrows). The tumor extends to invade the posterior wall of the urinary bladder with intraluminal tumor extension through the disrupted bladder wall (arrow heads). This proved to be anaplastic carcinoma of the cervix.
